newsitem.title: USA: Texas electric deregulation bill dies in House.
newsitem.headline: Texas electric deregulation bill dies in House.

text.p: A bill that would have opened the Texas electric grid to retail competition by the year 2002 died without a vote in a Texas House of Representatives committee on Tuesday, lobbyists said.

State Rep. Mark Stiles planned to pull his bill out of the House State Affairs committee, where the legislation stalled after regional electric co-operatives came out against the proposal last week, the lobbyists said.
"Stiles is going to pull it down this afternoon," said Bill Miller of the Texas Coalition for Competitive Electricity, which represents large industrial customers.

The compromise bill would have opened markets to competition on January 1, 2002, cut residential rates by 10 percent, frozen commercial rates and allowed utilities to recover stranded costs by depreciation and securitization.

But Stiles, a Beaumont Democrat, was unable to garner support from the co-ops, independent power marketers and large commercial customers that lined up against the bill over the weekend, the lobbyists said.
"I don't think he had the support. I don't think he had the votes in the commmittee to get it out," said Mickey Moore, a lobbyist with the Texas Retailers Association.
"Sadly for all Texas consumers -- large and small -- competition in electricity is dead for this legislative session," Stiles said in a statement. "We have simply run out of time."

An earlier Senate bill died after state utilities, power marketers and industrial customers failed to reach agreement on several key issues, including stranded cost recovery and a "date certain" to open the retail market to competition.
The state's largest utilities opened the legislative session opposed to deregulation, then began pushing for a bill after regulators signalled plans to cut rates, lobbyists said.

With the biennial state legislature set to adjourn on June 2, the Texas electric grid will remain open to wholesale competition but utilities will retain monopoly control over the retail market for at least another two years, lobbyists said.
But electricity traders said waiting two years for retail competition to begin in Texas was better than rushing a flawed deregulation bill through in the final weeks of the session.

"It was a bad bill," a Houston trader said. "The better- case scenario is that deregulation happens in California and in two years the committee reconvenes and there is immense public pressure for an immediate bill at that time."
California is leading the nation in the move to deregulate its electricity industry, breaking up utilities' traditional monopolies by introducing retail competition among power suppliers.

Texas also has emerged as a key state in the emerging deregulated electric industry, with Houston-based natural gas companies leveraging their trading expertise and back-room investments to form national electric wholesale operations.
